summary: Two discrete, market-relevant events cluster at the end of the window: Puerto Rico's governor announced the Commonwealth would default on a $422 million bond payment due Monday, with Congress unable to pass a restructuring bill (Day 12), and Donald Trump won the Indiana Republican primary on the flagged day (Day 14), following his sweep of five northeastern primaries a week earlier (Day 7). Alongside these, an emerging-market stress signal is visible in the Philippines, where the peso was described as Asia's worst-performing currency (Day 8) and the equity market suffered its biggest drop in months on Day 13. No single item describes a systemic macro shock, so the case rests on the accumulation of political and credit-event risk rather than one unambiguous trigger.
mechanism: A sovereign-style default by a US territory injects repricing and headline risk into municipal and credit markets, while a decisive primary result narrows the distribution of US election outcomes and forces political-risk premia to be re-marked; election-driven currency and equity stress in the Philippines shows the same uncertainty channel already operating in an emerging market.

claims.claim: Puerto Rico's governor announced the Commonwealth would default on a $422 million bond payment due the following Monday, having suspended debt payments to fund essential services, with Congress unable to pass a debt restructuring bill.
Donald Trump won the Indiana Republican presidential primary on the day the model flagged.
Trump had already been forecast to win Republican primaries in five states earlier in the window.
The Philippine peso was reported as the worst-performing currency in Asia because of a volatile and unpredictable presidential election.
The Philippine stock market suffered its biggest drop in months amid election uncertainty on Day 13.
Spain failed to form a government, forcing the king to dissolve parliament and call an unprecedented repeat election.
Iraqi officials declared a state of emergency for all of Baghdad after protesters stormed parliament in the Green Zone.
A Kuwaiti oil workers' strike that had cut the country's crude production by nearly half ended at the start of the window.
UK retailer British Home Stores, employing 11,000 people, collapsed into administration in the biggest high-street failure since Woolworths.
The Finnish parliament debated a citizen petition on abandoning the euro amid a weakening economy, though the petition was judged unlikely to lead to exit.

competing_explanation: The window is dominated by geopolitical and human-interest items with no direct pricing channel, and the financially relevant items are individually small or localised: the Puerto Rico default was pre-announced and long anticipated given Congress's failure to act, the Philippine moves are country-specific election noise, and a primary win in one US state changes no policy. On that reading the model may simply have flagged noise, or reacted to an oil-supply narrative (the end of the Kuwaiti strike restoring roughly half of a producer's output, plus emergency conditions in Baghdad) that the items describe only obliquely.
